narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest positive factor for you. At 3.40 it sits noticeably above the average of students who were admitted, and the model saw this as meaningful evidence that you could succeed. Unfortunately, two other factors pulled more strongly in the opposite direction.

Your class ranking at the end of your first year and again at the end of your third year both placed you in the second decile—well below the average sixth-decile ranking of admitted students. These consistently lower relative standings outweighed the benefit of your solid GPA and became the dominant reasons the model leaned toward predicting failure.

Your family income, LSAT score of 33, full-time study plans, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome; the model focused almost entirely on the academic-performance signals above.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score and, if possible, strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a master’s program that demonstrates higher performance in a competitive environment. These steps would directly address the factors that most influenced the current prediction. (248 words)
